also_known_as: Ruminal tympany; Afara (Hindi); frothy bloat; free gas bloat
required_image_view: Side (LEFT side preferred); rear view helpful
regions_to_inspect: Left paralumbar fossa (hollow between last rib, hip bone and spine); dorsal outline of the abdomen; head and mouth
key_visual_signs: Left paralumbar fossa filled and BULGING outward instead of hollow; upper left abdomen rising to or ABOVE the level of the backbone; tense drum-like left flank; abdomen asymmetrically larger on the left side when seen from behind
supporting_visual_signs: Neck and head extended; mouth open breathing; tongue protruding; drooling saliva; in severe cases both flanks distended; frequent small defecation and urination
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Restless, kicking at belly, getting up and lying down; standing with forelimbs on higher ground; abducted elbows; severe cases staggering or recumbent
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Late pregnancy: distension is LOW and on the RIGHT/ventral abdomen, fossa not bulging above spine. Well-fed full rumen: fossa filled but flat, not tense or above spine line. Vagal indigestion: 'papple' shape from behind (left upper + right lower distension), chronic. Obesity: fat evenly distributed, fossa not tense. Hydrops of uterus/allantois: bilateral pear-shaped lower abdomen in pregnant cow
signs_that_argue_against: Clearly visible hollow (sunken) left paralumbar fossa; calm cow eating or ruminating; distension only in lower belly
minimum_evidence_to_report: Left paralumbar fossa visibly distended and bulging to or above the backbone line
confidence_rules: HIGH: left fossa bulging above spine plus distress sign (open mouth, extended neck). MEDIUM: fossa clearly filled and convex but no distress. LOW: only right side visible or abdomen large but fossa not assessable
severity_and_urgency: Emergency if breathing distress or open-mouth breathing (death possible within hours). Moderate if only flank distension
risk_context: Sudden access to lush legumes (berseem, lucerne), wet green fodder, grain overload, choke (obstruction of oesophagus), tetanus, milk fever
farmer_question: Is your cow eating less? Is your cow's stomach enlarged?
image_quality_needed: Full-body side image, left side, cow standing, whole abdomen and backline in frame, camera at mid-body height
confirmatory_action: Vet exam; pass stomach tube to differentiate frothy vs free gas; do not delay if distress
notes_for_model: Cannot tell frothy vs free gas from image. If only the right side is visible, state that the left flank is needed and lower confidence. Check for tetanus signs (stiff tail, erect ears) because bloat is common in tetanus

also_known_as: Traumatic reticuloperitonitis; hardware disease; foreign body syndrome; traumatic reticulitis; traumatic pericarditis (complication)
required_image_view: Side; front view helpful for brisket
regions_to_inspect: Backline; elbows; forelimb stance; left flank fill; brisket and dewlap; jugular vein in neck
key_visual_signs: Arched back (kyphosis) with ABDUCTED ELBOWS (elbows turned outward away from chest); tucked-up abdomen; reluctance to move; stance with forelimbs placed on higher ground
supporting_visual_signs: Sunken left paralumbar fossa (poor rumen fill); mild recurrent bloat; dull coat; weight loss. If traumatic pericarditis: swelling (oedema) of brisket and dewlap, distended jugular veins along the neck
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Stiff, careful gait; reluctant to walk downhill or turn; grunting when lying down or getting up; stands for long periods; head and neck extended
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Laminitis: arched back but shifting weight between feet, pain in hooves, elbows not abducted. Abomasal ulcer: dark tarry dung. Pleuritis/pneumonia: nasal discharge, abdominal breathing. Ketosis: thin, no pain posture. Tetanus: rigid sawhorse stance with raised tail and erect ears. Hygroma or carpal lesions cause abnormal forelimb stance without arched back
signs_that_argue_against: Straight backline with elbows close to chest; normal alert walking; well-filled rumen
minimum_evidence_to_report: Arched back PLUS abducted elbows, OR arched back plus brisket oedema with distended jugular
confidence_rules: HIGH: arched back + abducted elbows + brisket/dewlap oedema. MEDIUM: arched back + abducted elbows. LOW: arched back alone (many causes). Never report HIGH from a single sign
severity_and_urgency: Moderate to severe; brisket oedema (pericarditis) indicates advanced and often poor prognosis
risk_context: Feeding chaffed fodder contaminated with wire, nails; common in Indian stall-fed and stray cattle eating from garbage; late pregnancy and calving increase risk
farmer_question: Is your cow eating less? Is your cow reluctant to move forward?
image_quality_needed: Full-body side image standing on flat ground, legs and backline visible; front view for brisket
confirmatory_action: Vet exam: withers pinch test, grunt test, metal detector, rumen magnet, ultrasound or radiography
notes_for_model: Visual signs are non-specific; phrase output as 'suspected' and ask the farmer question. Report brisket oedema separately if seen

also_known_as: Actinomycosis; Actinomyces bovis osteomyelitis; big jaw
required_image_view: Face (side profile of head) and side
detectable_from_side_image: Partial (only if head is large in frame)
regions_to_inspect: Lower jaw (mandible) especially at level of cheek teeth; upper jaw (maxilla); cheek; skin over swelling
key_visual_signs: Hard, bony, immovable swelling of the lower or upper jaw bone, causing obvious facial asymmetry; swelling appears continuous with the bone; one or more draining tracts (openings) discharging thick yellow pus with small gritty 'sulphur granules'
supporting_visual_signs: Skin over swelling hairless, scabbed or ulcerated; slow-growing (weeks to months); loose or misaligned teeth; drooling; weight loss in chronic cases
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Difficulty chewing, dropping feed (quidding); otherwise alert
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Soft-tissue abscess: soft, fluctuant, movable, not attached to bone, grows fast. Wooden tongue: tongue hard and swollen, soft tissue of throat affected, jaw bone normal. Bottle jaw: soft pitting oedema under the jaw (intermandibular space), bilateral, due to worms or low protein. Enlarged submandibular/parotid lymph node: round, behind or under jaw, not bony. Tooth root abscess, bone tumour, LSD nodules (multiple, whole body)
signs_that_argue_against: Soft, rounded swelling below (not on) the jaw bone; bilateral symmetrical swelling; rapid onset in days
minimum_evidence_to_report: Visible firm swelling located ON the mandible or maxilla creating facial asymmetry
confidence_rules: HIGH: bony jaw swelling + draining tract. MEDIUM: bony-looking jaw swelling without tract. LOW: swelling where bone vs soft tissue cannot be judged
severity_and_urgency: Chronic, non-emergency; progressive and hard to cure if advanced
risk_context: Coarse, spiny fodder, erupting teeth in young adults, mouth injuries
farmer_question: Is your cow eating less? Is there any swelling in your cow's face?
image_quality_needed: Close side profile of the head, both jaws visible, good light, ideally both sides for symmetry comparison
confirmatory_action: Vet exam: palpation, radiograph, pus smear for granules; treatment with sodium iodide and antibiotics
notes_for_model: Sheet notes that an abscess photo was actually lumpy jaw; always check whether the swelling sits on bone before choosing abscess

also_known_as: Circling disease; Listeria monocytogenes encephalitis; silage sickness
regions_to_inspect: Ears, eyelids, lips and muzzle for one-sided droop; tongue; saliva; head position; body position
key_visual_signs: ONE-SIDED facial paralysis: drooping ear, drooping upper eyelid, drooping lip on the same side; muzzle pulled toward the normal side; tongue hanging out of mouth; continuous drooling of saliva
supporting_visual_signs: Feed packed in the cheek on the paralysed side; head tilted; cloudy eye (exposure keratitis) on paralysed side; dull, depressed look
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Walking in circles to one side; leaning or pressing head against wall or post; incoordination; recumbent in late stage with paddling
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Otitis media/interna: ear droop and head tilt but cow bright, no drooling or circling. Polioencephalomalacia: blindness, star gazing, head held back, both sides. Rabies: bellowing, aggression, straining, progressive paralysis (zoonotic). Wooden tongue: tongue hard and swollen, not flaccid. FMD: drooling with blisters/erosions in mouth, no facial droop. Choke: drooling with bloat, neck extended. Lead poisoning: blindness, head pressing, convulsions
signs_that_argue_against: Face symmetrical (ears, eyelids, lips level on both sides); alert cow; oral blisters present
minimum_evidence_to_report: Asymmetrical face (unilateral droop of ear or eyelid or lip) with tongue protrusion or drooling
confidence_rules: HIGH: unilateral droop of 2 or more of ear/eyelid/lip + tongue out or drooling. MEDIUM: one-sided droop + drooling. LOW: drooling or tongue out only
severity_and_urgency: Urgent; needs antibiotic treatment early. Zoonotic: handle with gloves; rule out rabies
risk_context: Feeding poor quality or spoiled silage; winter/spring; adult cattle
farmer_question: Is your cow eating less? Is the tongue hanging from your cow's mouth?
image_quality_needed: Straight front view of face showing both ears and eyes level; side view of full body for posture
confirmatory_action: Urgent vet exam, neurological assessment; CSF analysis; start antibiotics early
notes_for_model: Compare left and right side of face carefully; head tilt in the photo can mimic ear droop, so compare eyelids and lips too

also_known_as: Acetonaemia; subclinical/clinical ketosis; nervous ketosis; fatty liver complex
detectable_from_side_image: Partial (as risk flag via body condition)
regions_to_inspect: Body condition: spine, ribs, hook and pin bones, tailhead, short ribs (loin); left paralumbar fossa fill; udder size; coat
key_visual_signs: Low body condition score (BCS 2 or below on 1 to 5 scale): individual ribs clearly visible, sharp spine and short ribs, prominent hook and pin bones, deep hollow around tailhead, sunken paralumbar fossa; in an EARLY LACTATION cow (large udder, recently calved)
supporting_visual_signs: Rapid visible weight loss; dull rough coat; empty (sunken) left flank indicating low feed intake; dry firm dung balls
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Dull, eats roughage but refuses concentrate; nervous form: excessive licking of skin or objects, chewing movements, head pressing, aggression, staggering
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Underfeeding or starvation: whole herd thin, not linked to early lactation. Parasitism/liver fluke: bottle jaw, anaemia. Johne's disease: chronic diarrhoea, not linked to calving. TRP: arched back, abducted elbows. Left displaced abomasum: similar appearance, needs 'ping' test. Tuberculosis: chronic cough. Breed type: dairy breeds (HF, Jersey) are naturally more angular than zebu
signs_that_argue_against: BCS 3 or more with good rumen fill; dry cow not in early lactation
minimum_evidence_to_report: Lactating cow (visible developed udder) with BCS 2 or below and sunken left flank
confidence_rules: Maximum confidence MEDIUM from image alone. MEDIUM: early lactation + BCS 2 or below + empty rumen + dull. LOW: thin cow only. Always label as 'ketosis suspected, confirm with test'
severity_and_urgency: Moderate; nervous signs are urgent
risk_context: First 2 to 6 weeks after calving, high yielders, fat cows at calving that lose weight rapidly, twin pregnancy (pregnancy toxaemia), poor energy diet
farmer_question: Is your cow eating less? Did your cow calve in the last 6 weeks?
image_quality_needed: Full side view and rear view, cow standing square, no blanket; good light to show ribs and bones
confirmatory_action: Rothera test or ketone strip on urine or milk; blood BHB meter; vet treatment with dextrose, propylene glycol
notes_for_model: Sheet criterion: body condition score less than 2. Report estimated BCS in the output. Do not diagnose ketosis in a thin dry cow or a bull

also_known_as: Scours; loose motion; enteritis; dysentery (if bloody)
regions_to_inspect: Tail, perineum, back of the thighs, hocks and hind legs; dung on ground; eyes (dehydration); coat
key_visual_signs: Liquid or watery dung soiling the tail, perineum and back of hind legs with vertical streaks running down to hocks; watery or pipe-stream dung on ground; wet, matted tail
supporting_visual_signs: Dehydration: sunken eyes with gap between eyeball and lid, dry muzzle, tight/tented skin, dull hair; weight loss. Colour clues: black tarry = upper gut bleeding (abomasal ulcer); fresh blood or mucus = dysentery (coccidiosis, salmonellosis, BVD, winter dysentery); yellow-white pasty in calves = calf scours; green frothy = grain or lush pasture
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Straining (tenesmus) with arched back and raised tail; weakness; recumbent if severely dehydrated
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Mild soft dung on lush pasture: minimal soiling, cow bright. Mud or dried dung on legs from dirty housing: dried, patchy, not fresh streaks. Urine staining: yellow stain below vulva, no faecal material. Vaginal/uterine discharge (metritis): pus or mucus from vulva, stringy, not dung. Blood from vulva after calving
signs_that_argue_against: Clean dry tail and hindquarters; formed dung pats on ground
minimum_evidence_to_report: Fresh liquid faecal soiling of tail and hind legs, or watery dung visible
confidence_rules: HIGH: fresh liquid soiling + watery dung visible. MEDIUM: fresh soiling only. LOW: old dried soiling (could be dirty housing)
severity_and_urgency: Urgent if blood in dung, severe dehydration (sunken eyes), calf, or recumbent
risk_context: Sudden feed change, grain overload, worms, coccidiosis in calves, infections (salmonella, BVD, Johne's), toxins
farmer_question: Is your cow having loose motion?
image_quality_needed: Side view showing hind legs, plus rear view of tail and perineum
confirmatory_action: Dung examination for worms, coccidia; oral or IV rehydration; vet if blood or dehydration
notes_for_model: Always report dung colour and dehydration signs if visible; note any blood specifically

also_known_as: Radial paralysis; dropped elbow; brachial nerve injury
regions_to_inspect: Elbow height compared with opposite forelimb; carpus (knee); fetlock; hoof position
key_visual_signs: On one FORELIMB: elbow dropped lower than the other elbow; carpus (knee) and fetlock flexed; limb held behind the normal position with the toe or the front (dorsal) surface of the hoof resting on the ground; limb cannot bear weight
supporting_visual_signs: Limb appears longer than the other; abrasion on the front of the fetlock or hoof from dragging; wasting of triceps muscle behind the shoulder in chronic cases
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Dragging the toe when walking; stumbles; unable to advance or extend the limb; three-legged lameness
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Humerus or elbow fracture: swelling, limb swinging abnormally, extreme pain. Brachial plexus injury: whole limb flaccid, shoulder also dropped. Knuckling of fetlock from contracted tendons (calves) or flexor injury: elbow NORMAL height. Sole ulcer or foot abscess: cow rests toe but elbow position normal and can extend limb. Shoulder lameness
signs_that_argue_against: Both elbows at same height; cow bearing weight normally
minimum_evidence_to_report: Dropped elbow on one forelimb with flexed carpus/fetlock
confidence_rules: HIGH: dropped elbow + knuckled fetlock + toe dragging on one forelimb. MEDIUM: knuckled forelimb fetlock with elbow position unclear. LOW: forelimb lameness only
severity_and_urgency: Moderate; mild cases recover in weeks; complete injury has guarded prognosis
risk_context: Prolonged lying on one side on hard floor (after surgery, milk fever, casting), trauma to shoulder, humerus fracture
farmer_question: Is your cow having trouble walking?
image_quality_needed: Side view with both forelimbs visible from shoulder to hoof, cow standing on flat surface
confirmatory_action: Vet exam for fracture; supportive splint, anti-inflammatories, padded bedding
notes_for_model: Distinguish from D08 Knuckling of fetlock: radial paralysis = forelimb with DROPPED ELBOW

also_known_as: Fetlock knuckling; contracted flexor tendons (calves); peroneal (fibular) nerve paralysis (hind limb); flexural deformity
regions_to_inspect: Fetlock and pastern of all four limbs; hoof angle; hock angle in hindlimbs
key_visual_signs: Fetlock joint bent FORWARD so that the pastern is upright or tilted forward and the animal stands on the toe tip or on the front (dorsal) surface of the hoof; front of fetlock abraded
supporting_visual_signs: Calves: often bilateral forelimbs from birth (contracted tendons). Adult hindlimb (peroneal paralysis): hock over-straightened (extended) with fetlock knuckled; hoof wall wear on the front; swollen fetlock
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Stumbling, dragging toe, walking on front of hoof; may correct momentarily when forced to walk
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Radial nerve paralysis: forelimb with dropped elbow. Upward fixation of patella: whole hind limb locked straight and pushed backward. Achilles rupture: hock DROPPED (lower), not straightened. Laminitis or sole ulcer: toe-resting stance but fetlock not flexed forward. Overgrown hooves (slipper feet): long toe, fetlock sinks backward, not forward
signs_that_argue_against: Normal pastern angle with heel on ground
minimum_evidence_to_report: Fetlock flexed forward with animal bearing weight on toe or hoof dorsum
confidence_rules: HIGH: clearly knuckled fetlock with weight on dorsal hoof. MEDIUM: toe-standing with fetlock angle unclear. LOW: abnormal hoof position only
severity_and_urgency: Moderate; in calves mild cases self-correct, severe need splints
risk_context: Newborn calves (congenital), lying on hard surfaces after calving, calving injury, injection into nerve area, hind limb trauma
farmer_question: Is your cow having trouble walking?
image_quality_needed: Side view at ground level showing all four hooves and fetlocks clearly
confirmatory_action: Vet exam: nerve assessment; splinting, bandaging, physiotherapy
notes_for_model: Specify which limb (fore/hind, left/right if visible) is affected

also_known_as: UFP; patellar locking; stifle lock; common in bullocks and buffaloes
visual_detectability: High (when locked at time of photo)
regions_to_inspect: Stifle, hock and fetlock angles of each hind limb; hind limb position relative to body
key_visual_signs: One hind limb locked in rigid EXTENSION and stretched BACKWARD behind the body; stifle and hock straight and cannot flex; fetlock flexed with the front of the hoof resting or dragging on ground
supporting_visual_signs: Abrasion on front of hind hoof or fetlock from dragging; intermittent (limb may unlock suddenly with a jerk); may affect both hind limbs
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Limb dragged behind while walking; sudden release with jerky movement; worse when starting to walk after rest, or when walking backward it may release
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Peroneal (fibular) nerve paralysis: hock extended and fetlock knuckled but limb not locked backward and can be flexed passively. Spastic paresis (Elso heel): young animal, straight hock, limb swings backward and upward off ground, gastrocnemius tense. Achilles rupture: hock dropped. Hip dislocation: limb shortened, hip asymmetry. Fracture: swelling and abnormal angulation
signs_that_argue_against: Hind limbs flexing normally at hock and stifle
minimum_evidence_to_report: Hind limb fixed straight and extended backward with toe dragging
confidence_rules: HIGH: hind limb extended backward + straight hock + dorsal hoof on ground. MEDIUM: straight hind limb extended caudally without clear toe drag. LOW: hind lameness only (intermittent condition may be missed)
severity_and_urgency: Moderate; responds well to medial patellar desmotomy surgery
risk_context: Common in Indian draught bullocks, buffaloes, poor body condition, straight hind limb conformation, working on uneven ground
farmer_question: Is your cow having trouble walking?
image_quality_needed: Side view with full hind limbs; a short video while walking is ideal because condition is intermittent
confirmatory_action: Vet exam: manual push of patella; medial patellar desmotomy
notes_for_model: Commonly found disease per sheet. A single photo may catch the limb unlocked; if farmer reports intermittent hindlimb dragging, mention UFP as possible

also_known_as: Gastrocnemius tendon rupture; common calcanean tendon rupture; dropped hock
regions_to_inspect: Hock height and angle; area just above the point of hock (calcaneus); hind digits
key_visual_signs: DROPPED HOCK: hock of one or both hind limbs sunk much lower than normal and over-flexed, at worst the hock nearly touching the ground (plantigrade stance, standing on the back of the lower leg); swelling above the point of hock
supporting_visual_signs: When only gastrocnemius part is ruptured: digits flexed ('crab claw' appearance); skin wound over tendon if trauma; muscle wasting of thigh
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Unable to bear full weight on affected limb; crouched hind stance if bilateral; difficulty rising
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Tibial nerve paralysis: mild hock drop, no swelling, fetlock knuckles. Tibia or calcaneus fracture: severe swelling, instability, abnormal angle. Hygroma of hock: swelling on side of hock but normal hock angle. Downer cow with gastrocnemius muscle rupture. Upward fixation of patella: hock STRAIGHT, not dropped
signs_that_argue_against: Normal hock angle and height matched on both hind limbs
minimum_evidence_to_report: Abnormally lowered and over-flexed hock on a hind limb
confidence_rules: HIGH: hock clearly dropped with swelling above the point of hock. MEDIUM: hock lower than opposite limb. LOW: hind lameness only
severity_and_urgency: Severe; poor prognosis in heavy adult cattle, especially if bilateral
risk_context: Slipping on wet floors, downer cow struggling, wounds from sharp objects, heavy cattle
farmer_question: Is your cow having trouble walking?
image_quality_needed: Side view with both hind limbs visible to compare hock heights
confirmatory_action: Vet exam, ultrasonography of tendon; casting or surgery in valuable animals
notes_for_model: Compare hock heights between the two hind legs in the image

also_known_as: Rupture of serratus ventralis muscle; dropped sternum; scapular displacement
required_image_view: Side; front and top views helpful
regions_to_inspect: Top edge of shoulder blade (scapula) relative to withers and backline; chest position between forelimbs; elbows
key_visual_signs: Top edge of one or both shoulder blades pushed UPWARD so it sticks out ABOVE the level of the withers/backline; chest appears to have sunk between the forelimbs
supporting_visual_signs: Elbows abducted (pointing outward); bilateral cases show both scapulae raised like 'wings'; recent fall or struggling
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Reluctant to walk; wide forelimb stance; shoulder rises further when weight is placed on that forelimb
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Zebu (Bos indicus) HUMP: normal fleshy, rounded, midline structure over withers in desi breeds (Gir, Sahiwal, Tharparkar, Ongole) and crossbreds; it is soft and in the midline, NOT a bony edge on the side. Thin cow: scapula prominent but NOT above spinous processes. Shoulder abscess or haematoma: soft swelling, not a raised bony edge
signs_that_argue_against: Scapula edge below or level with the withers; symmetrical midline hump in zebu breed
minimum_evidence_to_report: Scapular cartilage/edge visibly projecting above the dorsal spinous processes of the withers
confidence_rules: HIGH: scapula edge clearly above backline + lowered chest. MEDIUM: raised scapula in an image angle that could distort height. LOW: prominent withers only
severity_and_urgency: Moderate to severe; bilateral cases have poor prognosis
risk_context: Falls, slipping, rough handling, downer cows, vitamin E and selenium deficiency (nutritional myopathy)
farmer_question: Is your cow having trouble walking?
image_quality_needed: Side view at withers height; front view to compare both shoulders
confirmatory_action: Vet exam; serum CK, vitamin E/Selenium levels; confinement and supplementation
notes_for_model: VERY IMPORTANT in India: do not report a normal zebu hump as flying scapula. Identify breed type first

also_known_as: Lockjaw; Clostridium tetani infection
regions_to_inspect: Stance of all four limbs; tail; ears; third eyelid; nostrils and lips; left flank; any wound, castration or ring site
key_visual_signs: 'Sawhorse' stance: all four legs stiffly extended and spread apart; tail stiffly raised away from body ('pump handle tail'); ears erect and rigid pointing back; third eyelid protruding over the eye
supporting_visual_signs: Bloat (left flank distended) is very common; flared nostrils; retracted lips; head and neck extended; saliva drooling (cannot swallow); recumbent with legs rigidly extended and head bent back (opisthotonus) in late stage; recent wound, castration, dehorning, calving, nose ring or ear tag
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Stiff 'wooden' gait; cannot bend neck; exaggerated reaction to sound or touch; spasms; unable to open mouth
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Hypomagnesaemia (grass tetany): muscle tremors, paddling, convulsions, recent lush pasture. TRP: arched back, not rigid limbs. Laminitis: shifting weight. Polioencephalomalacia: blindness, star gazing. Strychnine poisoning. White muscle disease in calves: weak, not rigid. Meningitis
signs_that_argue_against: Relaxed tail hanging normally; ears mobile; flexing limbs while walking
minimum_evidence_to_report: Sawhorse stance with stiffly raised tail or rigid erect ears
confidence_rules: HIGH: sawhorse stance + raised stiff tail + erect ears or third eyelid protrusion. MEDIUM: sawhorse stance + one other sign. LOW: stiff stance only
severity_and_urgency: Emergency; high fatality; keep animal in quiet dark place
risk_context: Deep wounds, castration, dehorning, calving injuries, nose piercing, unvaccinated animals
farmer_question: Is your cow having trouble walking? Was there a recent wound, castration or calving?
image_quality_needed: Full-body side view showing tail, ears and all legs; close face image for third eyelid
confirmatory_action: Urgent vet: tetanus antitoxin, penicillin, wound debridement, sedation
notes_for_model: Also report bloat if present. Mention wound site if visible

also_known_as: Carpal hygroma; knee bursitis; hock bursitis; precarpal bursitis
regions_to_inspect: Front of carpus (knee) of forelimbs; lateral side of hock; other joints of legs
key_visual_signs: Round, well-defined swelling on the FRONT of the knee (carpus), less often on the outer side of the hock; size from a lemon to a football; joint shape behind it looks normal
supporting_visual_signs: Skin over swelling hairless, thickened or calloused; may be bilateral; usually little lameness unless infected; ulcerated or discharging if septic
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Usually walks normally; stiffness if very large; lameness if infected
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Septic arthritis: whole joint swollen all around, severe lameness, cow holds limb up. Cellulitis: diffuse swelling extending up/down the leg, hot and painful. Abscess: can be anywhere, often pointing with pus. Fracture: sudden, severe lameness. Tarsal cellulitis/hock sores: ulcerated hock skin from bedding. Tumour
signs_that_argue_against: No localised swelling at knee or hock
minimum_evidence_to_report: Well-circumscribed swelling over carpus or hock
confidence_rules: HIGH: round swelling over front of knee with normal limb function. MEDIUM: swelling over joint with lameness (could be septic). LOW: unclear leg swelling
severity_and_urgency: Mild to moderate; septic hygroma is more serious
risk_context: Hard concrete floors, poor bedding, repeated trauma while lying down; carpal hygroma in Indian cattle is linked to BRUCELLOSIS (zoonotic)
farmer_question: Is there any swelling in your cow's leg?
image_quality_needed: Side and front view showing knees and hocks
confirmatory_action: Vet exam; test for brucellosis (RBPT, ELISA) before draining; improve bedding
notes_for_model: Always add advisory: carpal hygroma may indicate brucellosis; handle discharge with gloves

also_known_as: Hypocalcaemia; parturient paresis; downer cow (at calving)
regions_to_inspect: Posture and head/neck position; udder; hindquarters; left flank; surroundings (newborn calf, placenta)
key_visual_signs: Cow lying on sternum (chest) with head and neck turned back and resting on her flank ('head tucked into flank' or S-shaped kink in neck); unable to rise; recently calved (full udder, calf nearby, placenta or discharge)
supporting_visual_signs: Dull, sleepy look; dry muzzle; dilated pupils; mild bloat; hind legs stretched out; in stage 3 lying flat on side with bloat. Stage 1 (standing): trembling, shuffling hind legs, stiff
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Cannot stand; makes no or weak attempt to rise; stage 1 staggering
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Calving paralysis (obturator nerve injury): hind legs splayed outward ('frog-legged'), cow alert. Downer cow syndrome: alert and attempting to crawl after calcium therapy. Toxic mastitis: a swollen hot or discoloured quarter, abnormal milk. Metritis/septicaemia: foul discharge. Hip dislocation or fracture: abnormal limb angle. Hypomagnesaemia: convulsions, paddling. Uterine prolapse: mass from vulva (check)
signs_that_argue_against: Cow standing and alert; not recently calved; heifer (rare in first calvers)
minimum_evidence_to_report: Recumbent adult cow around calving time with sternal posture and head turned to flank, or unable to rise
confidence_rules: HIGH: sternal recumbency + head to flank + signs of recent calving. MEDIUM: recumbent recently calved cow without head-to-flank. LOW: recumbent cow without calving evidence
severity_and_urgency: Emergency; responds dramatically to IV calcium if treated early; fatal in hours if untreated
risk_context: Within 72 hours of calving (mostly first 24 h), older cows (3rd lactation+), high yielders, Jersey and crossbreds, high calcium diet in dry period
farmer_question: Is your cow not getting up? Is your cow eating less? Did she calve recently?
image_quality_needed: Full side view of the recumbent cow including head, udder and hind legs
confirmatory_action: Immediate vet: IV calcium borogluconate; turn cow every few hours; blood calcium
notes_for_model: Check for uterine prolapse in the same image because it often co-occurs

also_known_as: Cancer eye; ocular SCC; bovine ocular squamous cell carcinoma
regions_to_inspect: Eyelids, third eyelid (inner corner), junction of cornea and white of eye (limbus), conjunctiva, periocular skin
key_visual_signs: Raised, pink-red, fleshy or cauliflower-like growth on the eyelid, third eyelid or at the edge of the cornea (limbus); early lesions are white raised plaques; late lesions are large, ulcerated, bleeding, necrotic masses
supporting_visual_signs: Tears and discharge; flies and foul smell; lack of pigment around the eye (white face, pink eyelids); older cow; one eye usually
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Rubbing eye, head shaking; otherwise normal
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Pink eye (IBK): central corneal ULCER and cloudiness, no fleshy growth, young animals. Warts (papilloma): dry grey horny growths on eyelid skin, young animal. Granulation tissue after injury. Lymphoma: eye bulging outward (exophthalmos) rather than surface mass. Eye worm (thelaziasis): worms in conjunctival sac, tearing. IBR conjunctivitis: white plaques on conjunctiva of both eyes with nasal discharge
signs_that_argue_against: No growth or plaque on eye structures
minimum_evidence_to_report: Visible proliferative mass or plaque on eyelid, third eyelid or limbus
confidence_rules: HIGH: fleshy or cauliflower mass at limbus/third eyelid/eyelid. MEDIUM: white plaque at limbus. LOW: only tearing or redness
severity_and_urgency: Moderate early, severe when large (can spread to lymph nodes); early surgical removal curative
risk_context: White-faced or unpigmented eyelids (HF crosses, Hereford), high sunlight (UV), older cattle; commonly found per sheet
farmer_question: Is there any excess tears from your cow's eye?
image_quality_needed: Sharp close-up of the eye(s) with lids open, good natural light, no flash glare
confirmatory_action: Vet exam, biopsy; surgical excision, cryotherapy, or enucleation
notes_for_model: Size and location of mass should be reported

also_known_as: Infectious bovine keratoconjunctivitis (IBK); New Forest eye; Moraxella bovis infection
regions_to_inspect: Cornea (clear front of eye), conjunctiva, eyelids, face below the eye
key_visual_signs: Excess tears with wet streak/staining running down the face below the eye; squinting (half-closed eye); red, inflamed conjunctiva; cloudy white or blue CENTRE of cornea, often with a white spot or crater (ulcer) in the middle
supporting_visual_signs: Blood vessels growing in from the edge toward the centre (red ring); bulging cone-shaped cornea in severe cases; one or both eyes; several young animals in herd affected
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Avoids sunlight, keeps eye closed, rubs eye, reduced grazing
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Ocular SCC: fleshy mass, older animal. IBR conjunctivitis: white plaques on conjunctiva, cornea opacity starts at edge, nasal discharge, fever. Malignant catarrhal fever: BOTH eyes with cloudiness starting at the edge (limbus), crusty muzzle, high fever, severe illness. Foreign body (grass awn) or trauma: one eye, object may be visible. Eye worm. Theileriosis also causes corneal opacity with enlarged lymph nodes
signs_that_argue_against: Clear cornea, no tear staining, eyes fully open
minimum_evidence_to_report: Central corneal opacity or ulcer, or tearing with red eye and squint
confidence_rules: HIGH: central corneal opacity/ulcer + tearing. MEDIUM: red eye + tearing + squint without visible cornea change. LOW: tear staining only
severity_and_urgency: Moderate; can cause blindness or corneal rupture if untreated
risk_context: Summer, flies, dust, tall grass, bright sunlight, young cattle, white face
farmer_question: Is your cow's eye red?
image_quality_needed: Close-up of eyes, eyelids open, natural light, no flash reflection on cornea
confirmatory_action: Vet exam, fluorescein stain; antibiotic eye treatment, eye patch, fly control
notes_for_model: Flash reflection can look like corneal opacity; check if bright spot is just glare

also_known_as: Pus pocket; subcutaneous abscess; injection site abscess
regions_to_inspect: Neck (injection sites), jaw, shoulder, flank, thigh, limbs, udder
key_visual_signs: Single (occasionally few) localised, rounded, dome-shaped swelling under the skin, often with a soft centre ('pointing') and hair loss at the top; may be discharging thick creamy yellow, green or white pus
supporting_visual_signs: Scab or opening at top of swelling; skin thinning; scar from old injection or wound nearby
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Usually normal; lameness if on limb; difficulty eating if near jaw
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Lumpy jaw: hard swelling fixed to jaw BONE. Haematoma: sudden appearance after trauma, soft, no pointing. Hernia (umbilical, flank): soft, may reduce when pushed, at typical sites. Hygroma: over the knee or hock specifically. LSD: many smaller firm nodules all over body. Enlarged lymph node: at fixed anatomical sites (in front of shoulder, flank fold, under jaw), often both sides. Warts: surface growth, rough. Tumour
signs_that_argue_against: Multiple widespread nodules (think LSD); swelling on jaw bone (think lumpy jaw)
minimum_evidence_to_report: Localised rounded swelling with pointing, hair loss or pus discharge
confidence_rules: HIGH: swelling with pus discharge or clear pointing. MEDIUM: single round swelling at common injection or wound site. LOW: swelling of unclear nature
severity_and_urgency: Mild to moderate; severe if near throat (breathing) or in udder
risk_context: Unhygienic injections, wounds, foreign bodies, Trueperella pyogenes infection
farmer_question: Is there any swelling on your cow's body?
image_quality_needed: Close-up of the swelling plus a wider shot showing its location on the body
confirmatory_action: Vet: needle aspirate to confirm pus, lance and flush, antibiotics if needed
notes_for_model: Report location of the swelling. Sheet notes a lumpy jaw image was in the abscess folder: check bone involvement

also_known_as: Lantana camara poisoning; hepatogenous (secondary) photosensitization; Ghaneri poisoning
regions_to_inspect: WHITE (unpigmented) skin areas on back, sides, udder, teats; muzzle; eyelids; ears; vulva; eyes and mucous membranes for yellow colour
key_visual_signs: Skin damage (redness, swelling, oozing, thick crusts, hard leathery skin that cracks and peels off in sheets) ONLY on WHITE / non-pigmented and sun-exposed skin, with a SHARP border where it meets black or brown skin, which stays normal; YELLOW (jaundiced) whites of eyes and gums
supporting_visual_signs: Swollen, drooping or curled ear tips; swollen eyelids and muzzle; raw ulcerated muzzle and tongue; cloudy eyes, tearing; peeling teat skin; weight loss; Lantana shrub (bushy plant with multicoloured flower clusters) seen in surroundings
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Seeks shade, restless, rubbing, kicking at udder; loss of appetite; constipation
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Dermatophilosis: 'paintbrush' crusts not limited to white skin, rainy season. Sunburn: mild, no jaundice. Ringworm: circular grey patches mainly on face and neck. Mange: itchy, thick wrinkled skin, hair loss. LSD: firm round nodules on all skin colours. FMD: blisters in mouth and feet. Burns, chemical irritation. Other photosensitizing plants or liver damage (fasciolosis, aflatoxins)
signs_that_argue_against: Lesions equally present on dark and white skin; all-black or all-dark cow with no mucosal jaundice
minimum_evidence_to_report: Crusting, peeling or swollen skin restricted to white patches with sparing of dark patches
confidence_rules: HIGH: lesions confined to white skin with sharp border + jaundice. MEDIUM: lesions confined to white skin, no jaundice visible. LOW: skin lesions on white skin but pattern unclear
severity_and_urgency: Severe; liver damage can be fatal; urgent removal from sun and from lantana
risk_context: Grazing on wastelands, forests and roadsides where Lantana camara grows (very common in India), drought or fodder scarcity, new animals unfamiliar with plant
farmer_question: Is your cow having any skin problem? Does your cow graze near lantana bushes?
image_quality_needed: Side view showing patches of white and coloured skin; close-up of muzzle, eyes and ears
confirmatory_action: Vet exam; liver function tests; house in shade; activated charcoal; supportive treatment
notes_for_model: The white-skin-only pattern is the single most useful clue. Also report jaundice, which overlaps with D30

also_known_as: Streptothricosis; rain scald; Dermatophilus congolensis infection; lumpy wool (sheep)
regions_to_inspect: Back and top of body (rain exposed), neck, shoulders, flanks, udder and teats, scrotum, perineum, lower limbs
key_visual_signs: Multiple raised, thick, crusty scabs with MATTED TUFTS OF HAIR sticking up ('paintbrush' lesions); crusts may join into large irregular crusted areas; when removed, a pink moist base with yellow-green pus is left
supporting_visual_signs: Scabs arranged in lines where rain runs down the body; greyish-brown crusts on udder and teats; heavy tick presence in same animal
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Usually not itchy; weight loss and weakness in severe generalized cases
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Ringworm: round, grey-white, ash-like flat crusts, mainly around eyes, face and neck, calves. LSD: firm round nodules within the skin, not matted-hair crusts, with fever and enlarged nodes. Photosensitization: limited to white skin. Warts: rough cauliflower-like growths. Mange: itchy, hair loss, thick wrinkled skin. Lice: hair loss and rubbing with visible lice
signs_that_argue_against: Smooth nodules; single circular lesions only on face
minimum_evidence_to_report: Several raised crusts with tufts of matted hair on dorsal body, udder or limbs
confidence_rules: HIGH: many paintbrush crusts in typical distribution. MEDIUM: crusted lesions without clear hair tufts. LOW: patchy skin lesions of unclear type
severity_and_urgency: Mild to moderate; severe generalized cases can cause death in calves
risk_context: Rainy, humid season; wet animals; tick infestation; skin damage by insects or thorns; crossbred animals
farmer_question: Is your cow having any skin problem?
image_quality_needed: Close-up of lesions and wider body shot showing distribution
confirmatory_action: Vet: smear of scab (Giemsa stain shows 'railway track' organisms); antibiotics; keep dry
notes_for_model: Sheet notes udder images; inspect udder skin carefully

also_known_as: Papillomatosis; bovine papillomavirus (BPV) warts; teat warts
required_image_view: Side, face; udder for teat warts
regions_to_inspect: Head (around eyes, ears), neck, dewlap, shoulders, whole body; teats and udder
key_visual_signs: Grey, white or dark, dry, rough, horny growths projecting from the skin, 'cauliflower' or fronded appearance; can be single, clusters, or hundreds; may join into large masses. On teats: small rice-grain, frond-like or flat round warts
supporting_visual_signs: Some warts on a stalk (pedunculated); bleeding or infection if damaged; usually young animals 6 months to 2 years
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Normally none; milking difficulty with teat warts
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: LSD: firm, smooth, round flat-topped nodules INSIDE the skin, sudden onset with fever, enlarged lymph nodes, whole body. Ringworm: flat grey crusty circles, not projecting growths. Dermatophilosis: crusts with hair tufts. Ocular SCC: growth on eye structures. Ticks: engorged ticks are smooth, grey, bean-shaped with legs near skin
signs_that_argue_against: Smooth, rounded skin nodules with intact hair (LSD)
minimum_evidence_to_report: One or more rough, cauliflower-like skin growths
confidence_rules: HIGH: typical cauliflower/fronded growths. MEDIUM: rough raised growths not fully typical. LOW: small bumps of unclear surface
severity_and_urgency: Mild; self-limiting in months in most young cattle
risk_context: Young cattle; shared equipment, fences, halters; group housing
farmer_question: Is your cow having any skin problem?
image_quality_needed: Close-up of growths showing surface texture
confirmatory_action: Vet: removal, autogenous vaccine if extensive
notes_for_model: Texture (rough horny vs smooth) is the key to separate warts from LSD

also_known_as: Ticks; Kilni/Chichdi (Hindi); Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus, Hyalomma, Haemaphysalis infestation
regions_to_inspect: Inside and edge of ears, neck, dewlap, brisket, armpits, belly, udder and teats, groin, inner thighs, around anus and vulva, under tail, tail switch
key_visual_signs: Visible attached ticks: small round or oval bumps on skin; engorged females are smooth, grey, bluish or brown, bean or seed shaped (up to about 1 cm); larger ticks with striped legs (Hyalomma) around udder, perineum, tail; clusters at predilection sites
supporting_visual_signs: Small bleeding spots, scabs and hair loss where ticks attached; rough coat; poor body condition; pale or yellow eyes if tick-borne disease present
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Rubbing, licking, restlessness
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Warts: rough surface, fixed growth. LSD nodules: firm, inside skin, larger and more widespread. Dried dung, mud or seed clumps stuck on hair. Flies: have wings, mobile. Skin tags
signs_that_argue_against: No attached parasites at predilection sites
minimum_evidence_to_report: At least one clearly visible attached tick
confidence_rules: Grade load: MILD fewer than 10 visible; MODERATE 10 to 50; HEAVY more than 50 or dense clusters. HIGH confidence when ticks are clearly in focus
severity_and_urgency: Mild to moderate by itself; heavy load causes anaemia and transmits babesiosis, theileriosis, anaplasmosis
risk_context: Warm humid season; crossbred and exotic cattle more affected; poor pasture management
farmer_question: Do you see ticks on your cow?
image_quality_needed: Close-up of ears, dewlap, udder, perineum and tail base in good light
confirmatory_action: Acaricide treatment (spray or pour-on); treat environment; check for tick-borne diseases
notes_for_model: SUPPLEMENT CONDITION: evaluate on EVERY image and report alongside other diseases. If ticks present, raise attention to D29 and D30

also_known_as: Lumpy skin disease; Capripoxvirus infection; Gaanth rog (Hindi)
regions_to_inspect: Entire skin: head, neck, dewlap, trunk, legs, udder, perineum; prescapular (in front of shoulder) and prefemoral (flank fold in front of stifle) lymph nodes; legs and brisket for oedema; eyes and nose
key_visual_signs: MULTIPLE firm, round, well-defined raised skin nodules 0.5 to 5 cm across, flat-topped, spread over head, neck, body and legs, hair standing up on the nodules; appear suddenly and in large numbers
supporting_visual_signs: Enlarged lymph nodes visible as swelling in front of the shoulder and in front of the stifle; swelling (oedema) of legs, brisket and dewlap; later nodules develop central dead core ('sit-fast'), scabs, deep punched-out ulcers; tears, nasal discharge, drooling; lameness
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Dull, reduced feeding, reluctant to move due to leg swelling; milk drop
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Pseudo-LSD (bovine herpesvirus 2): superficial lesions with central depression, heal in weeks. Insect bites/urticaria (allergic): soft, sudden, disappear within hours. Warts: rough cauliflower surface. Dermatophilosis: crusts with hair tufts. Ringworm: grey flat circles. Abscess: single, fluctuant. Tick bites. Hypoderma (warbles): nodules only on back with breathing hole, cool season. Besnoitiosis. Photosensitization: white skin only
signs_that_argue_against: Only one or two lesions; rough cauliflower growths; lesions limited to white skin
minimum_evidence_to_report: Multiple (roughly 5 or more) firm, round skin nodules distributed over body
confidence_rules: HIGH: many nodules over body + enlarged prescapular node or limb oedema. MEDIUM: many typical nodules only. LOW: few nodules or unclear lesions
severity_and_urgency: Severe and NOTIFIABLE; isolate animal, report to government veterinarian; control vectors
risk_context: Outbreaks in India since 2019 (major 2022); spread by flies, mosquitoes, ticks; unvaccinated cattle; monsoon season
farmer_question: Is your cow having any skin problem? Does your cow have fever?
image_quality_needed: Full body side view with good light; close-up of nodules
confirmatory_action: Report to veterinary authority; PCR of nodule or scab; isolate; vaccinate (goat pox / Lumpi-ProVacInd) in-contacts
notes_for_model: If LSD is detected, explicitly check and mention enlarged prescapular lymph nodes (overlaps D29)

also_known_as: Foot and mouth disease; Khurpaka-Muhpaka (Hindi); aphthous fever
required_image_view: Open mouth; face; side (for feet and saliva)
regions_to_inspect: Tongue, dental pad, gums, inner lips, muzzle, nostrils; mouth corners for saliva; feet (between claws, coronary band); teats
key_visual_signs: Profuse ropy/stringy saliva hanging from the mouth; blisters (vesicles, fluid-filled) or raw red ulcers (erosions) on the tongue, dental pad, gums and lips; shreds of peeling skin on the tongue; blisters or erosions between the claws and at the hoof-skin junction
supporting_visual_signs: Foamy saliva around lips; teat blisters; lameness, shaking or kicking feet, lying down a lot; sudden milk drop; panting and rough hair coat in recovered animals ('hairy panters'); multiple animals affected at once
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Lip smacking, reluctant to eat or walk, rocking weight between feet
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Sheet remark: excess salivation may also be due to CHOKE, ULCER or FOREIGN BODY. Choke: drooling + bloat + neck extended, no mouth lesions. Foreign body in mouth (wire, bone stuck between teeth): object visible, one animal. Oral ulcers (trauma, BVD/mucosal disease): erosions without blisters, diarrhoea. Wooden tongue: hard swollen tongue. Listeriosis: one-sided facial paralysis. Rabies: drooling with behaviour change. Malignant catarrhal fever: bilateral eye cloudiness, crusty muzzle. Bovine papular stomatitis: raised flat red papules on muzzle, mild. Photosensitization/lantana: tongue ulcer + white-skin lesions
signs_that_argue_against: Drooling with normal pink tongue and gums; single animal with bloat and extended neck (choke)
minimum_evidence_to_report: Oral vesicles or erosions, OR excessive stringy salivation together with foot lesions
confidence_rules: HIGH: oral blisters/erosions + drooling (+ foot lesions). MEDIUM: drooling + lameness, mouth not visible. LOW: drooling only (report as 'excess salivation, cause unconfirmed' and list choke/ulcer/foreign body)
severity_and_urgency: Severe and NOTIFIABLE; highly contagious; isolate, report to government vet
risk_context: Unvaccinated herds (India vaccinates under NADCP), new animal introduction, animal markets, monsoon and winter outbreaks
farmer_question: Is there any excess salivation? Is your cow limping?
image_quality_needed: Open-mouth image with tongue visible in good light; close-up of feet between claws
confirmatory_action: Report to veterinary authority; sample vesicle fluid/epithelium for lab confirmation; isolate; soft feed, antiseptic mouth wash, foot care
notes_for_model: Never confirm FMD from saliva alone; always state differential of choke, ulcer or foreign body

also_known_as: Fly infestation; horn fly, stable fly, house fly, face fly, horse fly worry; fly-strike (myiasis)
regions_to_inspect: Back, withers, shoulders (horn flies); legs (stable flies); face, eyes and muzzle (face and house flies); belly; any wounds
key_visual_signs: Many visible flies clustered on the body: dark specks concentrated on back, shoulders and belly, on legs, or around eyes and nose; flies feeding on wounds
supporting_visual_signs: Fly-bite marks: small bleeding points, crusts, hair loss along belly midline and legs; tear staining with flies at eyes; MAGGOTS in wounds (myiasis) is severe
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Constant tail switching, skin twitching, head throwing, foot stamping, bunching together, reduced grazing
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Ticks: attached, no wings, do not move away; dirt or dung specks; black skin spots in black/white animals
signs_that_argue_against: No flies visible
minimum_evidence_to_report: Clearly visible cluster of flies on the animal
confidence_rules: Grade load: LOW fewer than about 50 visible; MODERATE 50 to 200; HEAVY more than about 200 or dense clusters (economic threshold for horn flies about 200 per animal). Report maggots separately as URGENT
severity_and_urgency: Mild to moderate; flies spread pink eye, mastitis, LSD; maggot wounds are urgent
risk_context: Monsoon and summer, poor dung disposal, wet bedding, wounds
farmer_question: Do you see many flies on your cow?
image_quality_needed: Side view in good light; close-up of back and face
confirmatory_action: Insecticide spray or pour-on, fly traps, manure management; wound care for myiasis
notes_for_model: SUPPLEMENT CONDITION: evaluate on EVERY image and report alongside other diseases

also_known_as: Prolapse of uterus; calving bed out; Bachedani bahar aana (Hindi)
regions_to_inspect: Vulva and area behind the cow; hanging mass; surface of mass; cow's posture
key_visual_signs: Large, bag-like red to purple mass hanging from the vulva, often reaching down to or below the hocks; surface covered with many round button-like or mushroom-like knobs (caruncles) that are pathognomonic
supporting_visual_signs: Placenta (membranes) may be attached; mass may be swollen, dirty with dung and bedding, torn or bleeding; dark purple to black colour when prolonged (necrosis); cow may be recumbent (milk fever often co-exists); newborn calf nearby
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Straining; restless or lying down; shock (weak, recumbent) in late cases
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Vaginal prolapse: smaller, smooth, pink round mass without caruncles, usually before calving (common in buffaloes). Cervical prolapse: ring-like folds. Retained placenta: grey-red strands or sheets of membrane hanging, no solid organ. Rectal prolapse: cylindrical red mass from ANUS (above vulva). Calving in progress: calf feet or head visible in a water bag. Bladder eversion: small, round, with urine drops
signs_that_argue_against: Nothing protruding from vulva; only membranes hanging
minimum_evidence_to_report: Large mass protruding from the vulva
confidence_rules: HIGH: large mass from vulva with visible caruncles. MEDIUM: large red mass from vulva, caruncles not visible (could be vaginal prolapse). LOW: small protrusion only
severity_and_urgency: LIFE-THREATENING EMERGENCY; call vet immediately; keep mass clean and wet, raise it to vulva level on a clean sheet, prevent cow from trampling
risk_context: Within hours of calving, difficult calving, milk fever (hypocalcaemia), older cows, retained placenta; commonly found per sheet
farmer_question: Is there any mass hanging from your cow's back?
image_quality_needed: Rear view showing vulva and mass; side view of whole cow
confirmatory_action: Emergency vet replacement under epidural anaesthesia, calcium therapy, antibiotics, oxytocin
notes_for_model: Distinguish uterine (caruncles, after calving) vs vaginal (smooth, before calving) prolapse explicitly in output

also_known_as: Bovine herpes mammillitis (BoHV-2); teat skin ulceration; pseudocowpox (related differential)
regions_to_inspect: Teat skin, udder skin
key_visual_signs: Teats swollen with blue-purple discolouration, blisters that break into raw ulcers, and THICK DARK brown to black scabs covering large areas of the teat; skin peeling
supporting_visual_signs: Several teats and several cows (often first-calvers) affected; udder skin may be involved; mastitis in affected quarters
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Cow kicks during milking, resents touching teats
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Pseudocowpox: RING or horseshoe-shaped scabs, less painful. FMD: vesicles on teats plus mouth and feet lesions. Teat warts: dry growths. Chapped teats: cracks, dry skin. Photosensitization: white teats only with jaundice. Dermatophilosis: crusts with hair tufts. Teat trauma: single cut. Black pox: ulcer at teat end only
signs_that_argue_against: Smooth normal teat skin
minimum_evidence_to_report: Ulcers or thick dark scabs on teat skin
confidence_rules: HIGH: extensive dark scabs and ulcers on multiple teats. MEDIUM: ulcers/scabs on one teat. LOW: teat skin change unclear
severity_and_urgency: Moderate; causes milking difficulty and secondary mastitis
risk_context: Rare in India (per sheet remark); cool season; spread by milker hands and insects
farmer_question: Know your cow's udder health: are there sores or scabs on the teats?
image_quality_needed: Close-up of all four teats from the side and behind
confirmatory_action: Vet: swab for virus; teat dips, gentle milking, isolation
notes_for_model: Sheet marks it as rare in India; require clear teat lesions before reporting

also_known_as: Inflammation of the teat; teat injury; teat oedema; teat fibrosis/stenosis
regions_to_inspect: Each teat: size, shape, length, colour; teat end; teat canal opening
key_visual_signs: One or more teats UNEVEN in shape or size compared with the others: swollen, thickened, reddened or deformed teat; hard ring or lump in teat
supporting_visual_signs: Teat-end damage (rough, everted, ringed teat end, hyperkeratosis); cracks or cuts; scabs; teat shortened or bent
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Pain during milking, milk flow difficulty from one teat
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Mastitis: the whole QUARTER (udder part above) swollen, not only the teat. Mammillitis: ulcers and dark scabs on teat skin. Teat warts. Supernumerary (extra) teats: small, normal-looking extra teat. Udder oedema: diffuse, both halves, teats appear short. Normal variation in teat size between front and rear teats
signs_that_argue_against: All teats symmetrical and similar in shape
minimum_evidence_to_report: One teat clearly swollen or deformed compared with the others
confidence_rules: HIGH: swollen red deformed teat with lesion. MEDIUM: uneven teat shape without other signs. LOW: minor size difference only
severity_and_urgency: Mild to moderate; can progress to mastitis or blind quarter
risk_context: Poor milking technique, faulty milking machine, teat trauma, dirty floors
farmer_question: Know your cow's udder health: is any teat uneven in shape?
image_quality_needed: Close-up of the udder from the side and rear with all four teats visible
confirmatory_action: Vet: teat examination, CMT for mastitis, teat cannula or treatment
notes_for_model: Sheet criterion: uneven shaped teats

also_known_as: Thanela (Hindi); clinical mastitis; gangrenous mastitis; udder infection
regions_to_inspect: Udder quarters for symmetry, size and colour; skin of udder; teats; milk if visible
key_visual_signs: One or more udder quarters visibly SWOLLEN and larger than the others (asymmetry), with red or purplish skin; abnormal milk (clots, flakes, watery, yellow or blood-tinged) if visible
supporting_visual_signs: GANGRENOUS mastitis: blue-black, cold skin of a quarter with sharp line between dead and live tissue, oozing, sloughing. CHRONIC: one quarter shrunken and smaller (atrophy/fibrosis). Teat of affected quarter distended; cow dull or recumbent in toxic form
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Kicks during milking, stiff hind gait, hind legs spread; recumbency in toxic mastitis
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Udder oedema: both halves swollen symmetrically, soft pitting swelling extending forward along the belly, around calving, first calvers. Full udder before milking: symmetrical, normal colour. Udder haematoma or abscess: localised lump. Udder cleft dermatitis: moist foul sore where udder joins belly. Thelitis: only teat affected
signs_that_argue_against: Symmetrical udder with normal skin colour
minimum_evidence_to_report: Clear asymmetry with one swollen/discoloured quarter, or visible abnormal milk, or gangrenous skin
confidence_rules: HIGH: swollen red/purple quarter + abnormal milk, or gangrenous quarter. MEDIUM: clear asymmetric swelling. LOW: mild asymmetry only (report as 'possible, confirm with CMT')
severity_and_urgency: Moderate to emergency (gangrenous and toxic forms)
risk_context: Poor milking hygiene, dirty wet bedding, teat injuries, high yielders, early lactation, flies
farmer_question: Know your cow's udder health: is the udder swollen or milk abnormal?
image_quality_needed: Side and rear view of the udder showing all four quarters; image of milk in strip cup if possible
confirmatory_action: California Mastitis Test (CMT), strip cup, milk culture; vet treatment
notes_for_model: Subclinical mastitis cannot be seen; always recommend CMT when udder issue suspected

disease_name: Pre Scapular Lymph node enlargement in theileriosis
also_known_as: Tropical theileriosis; East Coast fever-like; Theileria annulata; prescapular lymphadenopathy
regions_to_inspect: Area just in front of the shoulder blade (lower neck/shoulder junction); flank fold in front of the stifle (prefemoral node); below the ear (parotid node); eyes; skin
key_visual_signs: Visible oval swelling IN FRONT OF THE SHOULDER (prescapular lymph node) on one or both sides, from egg to fist size, in an animal WITHOUT generalized skin nodules
supporting_visual_signs: Swelling of prefemoral and parotid lymph nodes; ticks (Hyalomma) on the body; watery eyes and corneal cloudiness; pale or yellow eyes/gums; nasal discharge; fast breathing; weight loss; small skin haemorrhages
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Dull, reduced feeding, weakness, laboured breathing
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: LSD: enlarged prescapular nodes TOO, but with many firm skin nodules (sheet remark: similar to LSD). Abscess: single, may point and discharge, not at node site. Lymphoma (enzootic bovine leukosis): many enlarged nodes, older cattle, no fever/ticks. Tuberculosis. Trypanosomosis
signs_that_argue_against: No swelling in front of shoulder; widespread skin nodules (think LSD first)
minimum_evidence_to_report: Visible swelling at prescapular lymph node site with no LSD nodules, ideally plus ticks
confidence_rules: HIGH: prescapular swelling + ticks + pale/yellow eyes or corneal cloudiness. MEDIUM: prescapular swelling + ticks. LOW: prescapular swelling only
severity_and_urgency: Severe; high fatality in crossbred calves without treatment (buparvaquone)
risk_context: Summer and monsoon; crossbred HF and Jersey highly susceptible; Hyalomma ticks
farmer_question: Is there a swelling in front of your cow's shoulder? Does your cow have fever?
image_quality_needed: Side view with neck and shoulder well lit
confirmatory_action: Blood and lymph node smear for Theileria (Koch's blue bodies); vet treatment with buparvaquone
notes_for_model: Sheet remark says this can be skipped because it resembles LSD. Recommended handling: report under D30 haemoprotozoan group when LSD nodules are absent

also_known_as: Haemoprotozoan diseases; tick fever; red water (babesiosis); gall sickness (anaplasmosis); jaundice complex
regions_to_inspect: White of the eye (sclera), eyelid lining (conjunctiva), gums, vulva lining, white skin of udder/teats; urine if visible; ticks; lymph nodes; body condition
key_visual_signs: YELLOW colour (jaundice) of the white of the eye, eyelid lining, gums or vulva lining; OR very PALE (porcelain white) mucous membranes indicating anaemia; RED, dark brown or coffee-coloured urine (haemoglobinuria)
supporting_visual_signs: Heavy tick load; enlarged prescapular lymph node (theileriosis); corneal cloudiness and tearing (theileriosis); weakness, weight loss; bloody or red milk (leptospirosis); fast breathing
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Weak, lagging behind herd, recumbent, may become aggressive in cerebral babesiosis
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Within the group: BABESIOSIS = red urine + anaemia + jaundice + ticks. ANAPLASMOSIS = severe anaemia and jaundice WITHOUT red urine, older adults. THEILERIOSIS = enlarged lymph nodes + fever + eye cloudiness. LEPTOSPIROSIS = red urine in calves, abortion, blood-tinged milk (zoonotic). Outside the group: lantana/liver damage (jaundice + white-skin lesions), copper poisoning, postparturient haemoglobinuria (red urine after calving, phosphorus deficiency), bacillary haemoglobinuria, liver fluke (bottle jaw), trypanosomosis
signs_that_argue_against: Clean white sclera and pink mucous membranes; clear or straw-coloured urine
minimum_evidence_to_report: Yellow sclera/mucosa, or clearly pale mucosa, or red/coffee coloured urine
confidence_rules: HIGH: jaundice or red urine + ticks. MEDIUM: jaundice or pallor alone in a clear, neutral-light image. LOW: colour assessment in yellow-tinted or poor lighting. Report which sub-disease is most likely based on the pattern above
severity_and_urgency: Severe to emergency; red urine and severe pallor can be fatal within days
risk_context: Tick exposure, summer and monsoon, crossbred cattle, recent movement, flooding (leptospirosis)
farmer_question: Is your cow's eye colour yellow? Is the urine red or dark?
image_quality_needed: Close-up of eye with lower lid pulled down, in DAYLIGHT without yellow artificial lighting; image of urine if possible
confirmatory_action: Blood smear (Babesia, Theileria, Anaplasma), PCV/haemoglobin, urine test; leptospira serology; vet treatment (diminazene, imidocarb, buparvaquone, oxytetracycline)
notes_for_model: Sheet criterion: eye colour yellow. Warm lighting or camera white balance can make the sclera look yellow: compare with other white objects in the image before reporting. Normal sclera may have a little brown pigment; do not call that jaundice

also_known_as: Actinobacillosis; Actinobacillus lignieresii infection; timber tongue
regions_to_inspect: Tongue (size, surface, position); mouth; saliva; area under the jaw and throat (lymph nodes)
key_visual_signs: Tongue SWOLLEN, HARD and protruding from the mouth; nodules, ulcers or granulation lumps on the tongue sides and surface; profuse drooling
supporting_visual_signs: Swelling under the jaw and throat (submandibular and retropharyngeal lymph nodes); nodules on lips, cheek or nose; weight loss due to inability to eat; rapid onset (days)
posture_gait_behaviour_cues: Difficulty picking up and chewing feed, chewing movements, dropping feed; alert otherwise
look_alikes_and_how_to_differentiate: Lumpy jaw: hard BONY jaw swelling, tongue normal. Listeriosis: tongue hangs out LIMP (paralysed, not swollen) with one-sided facial droop. FMD: vesicles and erosions, peeling tongue skin, foot lesions, many animals. Foreign body in mouth: object visible. Tongue injury. Botulism: limp tongue, whole body weakness. Rabies. Choke
signs_that_argue_against: Normal sized soft tongue; drooling with visible blisters (FMD)
minimum_evidence_to_report: Swollen, firm-looking tongue protruding from mouth, or tongue nodules/ulcers
confidence_rules: HIGH: enlarged protruding tongue with nodules/ulcers + drooling. MEDIUM: protruding swollen tongue + drooling. LOW: drooling or tongue protrusion only
severity_and_urgency: Moderate; responds well to sodium iodide if treated early; starvation risk
risk_context: Coarse, stemmy, thorny fodder causing mouth wounds
farmer_question: Is your cow eating less? Is your cow's tongue swollen?
image_quality_needed: Open-mouth close-up with tongue visible, plus face side view for throat swelling
confirmatory_action: Vet: palpation (hard tongue), biopsy/culture; sodium iodide IV, antibiotics
notes_for_model: Compare with listeriosis (limp tongue) and FMD (vesicles) explicitly
